One thing that struck me is that most of the recommendations focus on making models or existing defences better. Those are key, but they still leave the model holding implicit authority over real-world actions.

Sources indicate that I wonder if we need to move the trust boundary instead. Rather than asking “did the model decide correctly?”, ask “does this action have explicit authority to execute?” If every consequential action (shell, filesystem, cloud APIs, payments, emails, etc.) had to cross an independent execution boundary that could verify authority before it happened, then improving models becomes one layer of defence rather than the only layer.

That feels like a more fundamental architectural shift than simply adding more safeguards to the model itself.

One thing that's applicable to many developers is that it demonstrates some of the risks of storing secret/sensitive configuration in environment variables. Environment variables are inherited by child processes, and a malicious child process can run env or look in /proc/[PID]/environ to see them.

Industry observers note that it's fine for dev, but shouldn't be done in prod. On a Linux system, systemd has some abstractions to properly deal with secrets (https://systemd.io/CREDENTIALS/ ). Most importantly, the secrets aren't visible to any other process (using mount namespacing), nor are they automatically passed to child processes. Access control is implemented in the kernel itself, and encryption can be handled a bunch of ways - using a key on a TPM chip, on disk, passed in via SMBIOS OEM strings, via a Cloud Instance Metadata Services (IMDS), etc.

Of course, there's other solutions for secret management too.

Recent findings suggest that A leitura da timeline técnica oficial da Hugging Face traz o choque de sobriedade que faltava ao debate: não foi ficção científica, foi falha básica de isolamento e fronteira de execução.Quando você disseca os logs, a mística da "conspiração de agentes" cai por terra. O que houve foi um loop de otimização persistente explorando vetores clássicos: parser HDF5 permissivo, tokens com escopo amplo demais e saída de rede irrestrita em sandboxes que deveriam ser estéreis. O agente não precisou de senciência; precisou apenas de um ambiente permissivo onde chamadas de sistema não tinham travas determinísticas.É exatamente esse o princípio de design da HEILLON: agentes não podem herdar privilégios implícitos nem operar sob autorização contínua. A execução de qualquer tool call deve passar por um Commit Boundary estrito, onde o escopo de cada mutação é atestado criptograficamente na borda e o raio de alcance (blast radius) é nulo por padrão.Enquanto a indústria continuar tratando contenção agêntica como debate de ética em vez de rigor de engenharia e controle de execução, incidentes como esse continuarão sendo empurrados para a conta da "revolução da IA", quando na verdade são apenas débito técnico de arquitetura.

I spent some time with this timeline and with Tailscale's later write-up, and the part that stuck with me is what that stolen enrollment key actually was.

Sources indicate that it wasn't a Tailscale vulnerability. The key did what it was designed to do: enroll a node into the mesh with the reach already assigned to a CI identity. That's network membership, not access to one named service. After a rooted production node had already joined, the agent made 181 more enrollments from an external sandbox. From there it could see what that identity was allowed to reach, and it did use those routes, including traffic out through the company's exit nodes and source control through the connector its tag allowed. Hugging Face found no evidence those enrolled nodes were used to reach a private workload or an internal Kubernetes API, which matters. The credential still let the agent place 181 nodes on the network.

Tailscale's own advice is the right starting point: prefer workload identity federation over a reusable automation key, and keep enrollment narrower when a key is still needed. I would also ask a prior question: did the job need network membership at all, or did it need one service?

I wrote up the longer version here: https://thirp.net/field-notes/the-credential-that-became-a-network/.

  • To scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients. However, physical and cost constraints make scaling a single slice increasingly difficult.

To scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters. However, when training across multiple datacenters over wide-area networks (WAN), standard data-parallel training suffers from severe network stalls because slow WAN transfers cannot be fully overlapped with computation.

It has been revealed that to address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections. In this blog post, we discuss the core concepts of DiLoCo, how it is implemented in MaxText (Google's open-source JAX-based LLM training framework), and the performance benefits it brings to large-scale LLM training on Google Cloud.

Industry observers note that diLoCo was introduced by Google DeepMind in the paper DiLoCo: Distributed Low-Communication Training of Language Models. Instead of synchronizing gradients across all devices at every single training step (as in standard Data Parallelism), DiLoCo partitions training across M independent compute groups, referred to as learners, and allows each learner to perform many local optimization steps independently before communicating across groups.

Despite communicating significantly less frequently (by a factor of H, e.g., 1-2 orders of magnitude less) than standard synchronous training, DiLoCo has been shown to achieve comparable convergence and model quality.

The Vanilla DiLoCo described above reduces total communication volume by a factor of H, however, all learners still transmit their weight deltas for the entire model all at once at every H-th step. On a thin network pipe, that full-model transfer creates a large periodic stall every H steps. This issue is alleviated by Streaming DiLoCo, which is described in the next section.

Industry observers note that in multi-slice training, communication within a single slice is handled by high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnects (ICI). When scaling to multiple slices, synchronization across slices must traverse the Data Center Network (DCN) or, if the slices are geographically distributed, wide-area networks (WAN).

Within a single datacenter, DCN bandwidth is high enough that JAX and XLA can often hide standard Data Parallel all-reduce collectives by overlapping gradient communication with backward-pass computation. Across datacenters or congested links, however, bandwidth drops and latency rises sharply. Standard DP stalls at every step waiting for global gradient synchronization, collapsing Model FLOPS Utilization (MFU).

Streaming DiLoCo eliminates this synchronization stall by partitioning the model's parameters into P disjoint fragments. Over the course of H steps, every single fragment in the model is synchronized exactly once, achieving the exact same outer-loop cadence as vanilla DiLoCo without spiky bandwidth utilization.

Using a roofline model (similar to the JAX Scaling Book), we can calculate the network bandwidth required to prevent communication stalls for a model with ∣Θ∣ parameters (at b bytes per parameter, e.g., b=2 for bfloat16) and per-step compute time tstep=tfwd+tbwd. For example, the standard Data Parallel algorithm transfers 2∣Θ∣b bytes per sync via an all-reduce collective, which is a distributed reduce-scatter where each node reduces a different part, followed by an all-gather so all participants receive all parts. To achieve zero communication stalls, we overlap the reduce-scatter of the gradients with the backward pass, which produces them and takes tbwd time. Therefore, the peak required bandwidth is Bdp ≈ 2∣Θ∣b / tbwd.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dutch developer Jordi Bruin rolled out an upgrade to his excellent transcription app MacWhisper this week with a much-requested feature: the ability to automatically identify previously named speakers in new recordings. Here are the details.

I’ve written multiple times in the past couple of years about how MacWhisper has become an integral part of my podcast post-production workflow for show notes, episode descriptions, and more.

Which is why I’ve followed the app’s development very closely, and Jordi’s efforts to make it an increasingly powerful tool for casual and power users alike.

In the last few months alone, MacWhisper got a completely redesigned transcript editor, real-time meeting transcription, significantly improved speaker detection, deeper integration with Apple Intelligence, Siri, and Spotlight, and support for multiple new transcription models.

This week, MacWhisper got updated to version 16, packing several improvements, chief among them the ability to recognize speakers based on their voices in previous transcripts.

Sources indicate that until now, while MacWhisper could distinguish between different speakers in a recording (a process known as speaker diarization), owners still had to assign names to each new transcription manually. With MacWhisper 16, that is no longer necessarily the case.

In a recent development, now, MacWhisper creates a set of voiceprints for the speakers customers have previously identified, and uses them as a reference when processing newly introduced recordings. Depending on the confidence level of a match, MacWhisper will either automatically assign the speaker’s name or ask the user to confirm their identity.

According to Bruin, as people transcribe more recordings featuring the same people, MacWhisper gets better at recognizing their voices. All voiceprint processing and storage happen on-device, which is a great touch.

The feature also works with existing transcripts, which is fantastic for longtime MacWhisper users such as myself. A new Voice Recognition section in the app’s settings lets users generate voiceprints from existing transcripts, clear a speaker’s stored voice data, or turn the feature off altogether.

Importantly, voice recognition also works with live meeting transcriptions, although automatic name assignments happen once the meeting ends.

The fresh feature requires a MacWhisper Pro license, an Apple silicon Mac, and on-device transcription with speaker detection enabled.

Creating high-quality visual content once meant specialized cameras, technical knowledge and hours of editing. Today, software does a growing share of that work. Cameras recognize subjects, adjust exposure, stabilize footage and hand clips to editing tools that transcribe, reframe and tag them.

Recent findings suggest that for developers and technical creators, the interesting part is how these features are built and where they fail. This article covers how computational photography prepared the ground, what on-device vision can and cannot do, how wearable cameras change capture, and how to add a small, tested quality check to your own media pipeline. It ends with the privacy and authenticity questions that come with building camera features. Product capabilities change swiftly, so check each vendor's current documentation.

In a recent development, digital photography made images easy to capture, review and share. Smartphones then folded capture, editing and publishing into one device. The next shift was computational photography: instead of relying only on the lens and sensor, the device combines several captures and processes them in software.

In a recent development, high dynamic range (HDR) imaging is the clearest example. A camera captures frames at different exposures and merges them so both bright skies and dark foregrounds keep detail. Research indexed on PubMed, published in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, examines how deep learning has advanced HDR imaging, particularly in reconstructing visual information across different exposure levels.

Machine learning extends this approach from merging pixels to understanding them, which is what lets a camera decide what is the subject and what is the background.

Most AI camera features fall into a few groups.

These tools make real-time features practical, since a round trip to a server would add delay. They also keep raw frames on the user's device, which helps with the privacy concerns discussed below.

Because of these failure modes, a pipeline should check what the camera produced before running expensive downstream steps.

A cheap pre-check can reject a frame that is too soft or badly exposed before you spend time on transcription, upscaling or model inference. The script below uses numpy and Pillow. It measures sharpness as the variance of a Laplacian, a standard blur indicator, and measures exposure as the share of crushed and clipped pixels.

The test builds a detailed random frame and a blurred copy, then checks that the sharp frame scores far higher, that a mostly black frame is flagged as underexposed and that a mostly white frame is flagged as overexposed:.

Run the tests with python3 test_frame_quality.py. In our run, the detailed test frame scored about 33,000 for sharpness and its blurred copy scored under 2.

It has been revealed that traditional capture means holding a camera, propping up a phone or setting up equipment. Wearable cameras let creators record from their own point of view while their hands stay free, which suits travel video, instructional content, outdoor activities and behind-the-scenes footage.

In a recent development, camera-equipped smart glasses are one form of this. Several makers sell them, and consumer listings such as ai glasses with camera show how the category is presented to buyers. Depending on the device, customers start recording with physical controls or voice commands. Specifications differ widely, so compare field of view, storage, battery life and software support before choosing one.

Industry observers note that for developers, wearables change the input. Footage is shaky, framed by head movement and often recorded outdoors, which is exactly where a quality check and stabilization matter. Battery capacity, camera position, storage and recording duration also limit extended productions. Wearables are an additional option for perspectives that are hard to reach otherwise, not a replacement for traditional cameras.

Editing involves reviewing clips, correcting color, adjusting audio and preparing videos for each platform. AI tools automate several repetitive parts of that work:.

It has been revealed that creative judgment stays human. Choosing meaningful moments, shaping narrative flow and keeping a consistent visual style are decisions software cannot reliably make. Real-time assistance during recording will depend on hardware, software and environmental conditions.

As cameras get smaller, responsible recording matters more. Wearable devices can capture footage without the obvious movements of a handheld camera, so people nearby may not know recording is happening. The European Data Protection Board has highlighted transparency, personal data protection and recording awareness as notable considerations for camera-equipped smart glasses.

According to recent reports, authenticity is the second challenge. AI tools can enhance an image, but heavy alteration can also mislead. The National Institute of Standards and Technology has examined technical approaches to digital content transparency, including provenance tracking, watermarking and synthetic-content detection. On the provenance side, the C2PA coalition publishes an open standard called Content Credentials, which helps show where content came from and what edits it has undergone.

Cameras will likely get better at faster subject recognition, more efficient automated editing and stronger low-light performance as computer vision and on-device computing advance. Wearables may widen first-person storytelling, and editing tools may make multi-platform publishing simpler. Technical gains alone will not decide quality, though. Originality, storytelling and thoughtful creative decisions still do.

Not always. Toolkits such as ML Kit face detection and Apple's Vision framework run image analysis on the device, which reduces delay and keeps frames local.

It narrows the gap in many conditions, but optics, sensor size and control still matter for demanding work, and AI enhancement can introduce artifacts of its own.

AI-powered cameras make photography and video production more accessible, efficient and flexible, from on-device subject recognition to automated editing and wearable capture. The same tools create new work for developers: checking output quality, handling their failure modes and building privacy and provenance into the product. Technology reduces technical barriers, but the creativity and judgment behind good content remain human.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The US Senate has unanimously passed a bill that would ban death, war and terrorism contracts on CFTC-registered prediction-market exchanges.
  • Adam Schiff and John Curtis are the sponsors of the DEATH BETS Act.
  • Under the measure, any exchange registered with the CFTC would lose the ability to list or clear contracts on a person’s death, terrorism, assassination, war or US military operations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US Senate has unanimously passed a bill that would ban death, war and terrorism contracts on CFTC-registered prediction-market exchanges. The vote would turn regulatory discretion into a statutory ban just as the CFTC proposes looser rules, and the House has only weeks to act.

Sens. Adam Schiff and John Curtis are the sponsors of the DEATH BETS Act. It is the first prediction-market bill the Senate has passed this Congress. The measure now heads to the House.

Under the measure, any exchange registered with the CFTC would lose the ability to list or clear contracts on a person’s death, terrorism, assassination, war or US military operations. Sports contracts are not covered.

Curtis made a moral case for the bill on the Senate floor. “There should be no financial incentive to profit from terrorism, war, or the death of another human being,” he noted.

Industry observers note that whether such contracts can trade currently rests on the CFTC’s discretion. The bill would replace that discretion with a prohibition written into statute.

According to recent reports, the timing puts lawmakers and the regulator on different tracks. CFTC Chair Selig prepares to rewrite the prediction-market rules. The agency’s proposed rule would amend Regulation 40.11 and add Appendix F to Part 40. The agency would use that framework to decide when a contract linked to war, terrorism, assassination, gaming or illegal conduct is against the public interest.

Recent findings suggest that that framework would give the agency more room, not less. The proposal would say only that the CFTC may find such contracts contrary to the public interest, dropping the categorical prohibitions in the current rule, according to the Congressional Research Service. The agency withdrew a stricter 2024 proposal in February 2026.

For exchanges, the difference is significant. An agency can revise a rule through its own process. A ban in statute would keep those categories off the table regardless of how the CFTC’s rules change.

Recent findings suggest that the DEATH BETS Act targets a specific set of contracts. Sports is a different matter for operators. Schiff and Curtis have also introduced the Prediction Markets Are Gambling Act. That bill would bar sports-betting and casino-style contracts on these exchanges.

It has been revealed that A unanimous vote on death and war contracts does not prove the same support exists for a sports ban. It does show that senators are willing to legislate directly on what prediction markets can list, rather than leave the question to the CFTC.

That makes the vote an early sign of how much support Congress has for limiting these platforms. It comes while the exchanges are fighting state gambling regulators in court. Operators now face pressure from state regulators, the CFTC’s rulemaking and Congress at the same time.

Industry observers note that the House now has a short window. So far, the chamber’s leadership has given no word on putting the bill to a floor vote, FinanceFeeds reported.

NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams: Bringing Real-Time Generative Simulation to Surgical Robotics

📅 27 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Surgical robotics is moving quickly from teleoperation toward increasingly capable vision-language-action policies.
  • Industry observers note that world foundation models offer a different path.
  • Today, we are introducing the next step: Cosmos-H-Dreams, a real-time, action-conditioned generative simulator for surgical robotics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Surgical robotics is moving quickly from teleoperation toward increasingly capable vision-language-action policies. But evaluating and training these systems remains difficult. Physical robotic platforms are expensive to operate, experiments are slow to reproduce, and failures can damage instruments or biological material. Conventional simulators provide a safer alternative, but surgical scenes are exceptionally difficult to model: deformable tissue, fine instrument interactions, specular surfaces, sutures, needles, smoke, and occlusions all matter.

Industry observers note that world foundation models offer a different path. Instead of manually authoring every object and physical interaction, they learn visual dynamics directly from synchronized video and robot kinematics. NVIDIA's Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator demonstrated this approach by generating future surgical video from an initial scene and a sequence of robot actions. It enabled faster-than-physical evaluation and synthetic data generation across the Open-H-Embodiment ecosystem.

Today, we are introducing the next step: Cosmos-H-Dreams, a real-time, action-conditioned generative simulator for surgical robotics. Cosmos-H-Dreams distills the capabilities of Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator into a causal, few-step student model and serves it through FlashDreams, NVIDIA's accelerated streaming-inference library. Running on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU, the result is an interactive environment that a person or a learned policy can control in a closed loop.

Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator is an action-conditioned world foundation model built on NVIDIA Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B and post-trained on the Open-H-Embodiment dataset. Given a surgical context frame and a future robot trajectory, it generates video showing the likely visual consequences of those actions. This makes it useful for offline policy evaluation and synthetic data generation. A recorded or policy-generated trajectory can be sent to the model, the corresponding rollout can be generated, and the result can be inspected or scored without repeatedly executing the motion on a physical robot.

Cosmos-H-Dreams moves the model into the real-time regime. Starting from the multi-embodiment surgical priors learned by Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator, we specialize the model for da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) tabletop suturing and distill it into a causal student that generates the scene autoregressively. The released model receives an initial RGB frame and a live stream of robot kinematics, then produces the next chunk of frames before continuing with the following action block.

We have also demonstrated the versatility of Cosmos-H-Dreams by collaborating with CMR Surgical and Cambridge Consultants to integrate it with the Versius surgeon controller, enabling real-time operation on the Versius platform.

The key challenge is preserving useful surgical dynamics while reducing the cost of generation. Cosmos-H-Dreams uses a teacher-to-student training pipeline designed for long, autoregressive rollouts.

The bidirectional teacher begins from the Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator Open-H checkpoint, which uses a unified 44-dimensional action representation. For the released dVRK tabletop model, the dual-arm dVRK action content, consisting of relative end-effector translation, rotation, and gripper state, is mapped into this common representation.

Sources indicate that the teacher is then fine-tuned on the JHU dVRK tabletop mixture, including successful demonstrations as well as failure and out-of-distribution episodes such as needle drops, missed throws, and unsuccessful knot ties. These failures are important: a simulator intended to evaluate policies must reproduce the consequences of poor actions, not only ideal demonstrations.

To improve stability during long rollouts, the training process progressively increases the teacher's temporal horizon. We start training on a 12-frame horizon and progressively increase this number until 72 frames. At each horizon bump, we initialize the warmed-up model with pretrained weights.

The teacher's denoising trajectories are first precomputed and cached. A causal student is initialized from the teacher and trained to imitate these cached trajectories. This warmup stage teaches the student to operate with causal attention and a streaming key/value cache before it begins learning from its own generated history.

It has been revealed that autoregressive models face a familiar problem: during training they may see clean, ground-truth context, while during deployment they must condition on their own imperfect outputs. Small errors can therefore compound over time.

Sources indicate that cosmos-H-Dreams addresses this mismatch with self-forcing distillation. During training, the student rolls forward using its own generated context. Distribution-matching supervision from the frozen teacher then guides those self-generated rollouts toward realistic surgical video. This prepares the student for the same conditions it will encounter during interactive inference.

Recent findings suggest that the resulting model supports few-step diffusion, with as few as two denoising steps per latent frame, rather than the many-step process used by the full teacher. It combines the teacher's surgical priors with the causal structure needed for streaming.

Model distillation is only part of the real-time story. Cosmos-H-Dreams is served through FlashDreams, an accelerated inference library for autoregressive world and video models.

FlashDreams turns the distilled student into a low-latency streaming system through several complementary optimizations, such as streaming KV cache, CUDA Graph capturing, or model compilation.

Together, these techniques bring the distilled surgical world model fine-tune from the roughly ten-frames-per-second regime of standard Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator inference to interactive operation (~160 frames per second) on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000.

Industry observers note that cosmos-H-Dreams also provides the human-machine interfaces that turn generation into interaction. A browser client can send keyboard commands and receive generated frames over WebRTC. A Meta Quest client can map tracked controller motion into robot actions and display the synthesized scene through WebXR. The same model can also be connected to a learned surgical policy, with generated observations and predicted actions exchanged inside a closed loop.

It has been revealed that while Cosmos-H-Dreams includes a pre-trained checkpoint for tabletop suturing, the system is designed to be extensible to your specific embodiment. To train a real-time student model for your own dataset, we provide a complete recipe for teacher fine-tuning and self-forcing distillation in our step-by-step guide.

Cosmos-H-Dreams opens a fresh frontier for surgical simulation: environments learned from real robot data that are responsive enough to be inhabited.

The immediate next step is to evaluate more than visual quality. A useful surgical simulator must respond correctly to actions, preserve instrument and scene structure over long rollouts, and support conclusions that transfer to the physical robot. This motivates a latest family of closed-loop benchmarks: tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action diversity, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and real policy outcomes.

It has been revealed that real-time world models can also become active partners in surgical policy development. They can generate rare failures on demand, provide scalable environments for reinforcement or imitation learning, and enable rapid evaluation of new policies without tying every experiment to scarce robotic hardware.

Recent findings suggest that further ahead, real-time simulation enables a series of downstream applications such as latency-aware telesurgery, where the world model helps maintain a more stable display; or interactive surgical rehearsal, procedure planning, and intraoperative decision support. Cosmos-H-Dreams is a research and development platform, not a diagnostic system, a replacement for intraoperative imaging, or a controller for a physical surgical robot. Yet it provides a foundation for exploring these possibilities safely.

As model fidelity, temporal stability, and hardware efficiency continue to improve, real-time generative simulation can help connect surgeon education, synthetic data generation, policy training, and policy evaluation within one shared Physical AI environment.

Cosmos-H-Dreams brings action-conditioned surgical world modeling into the real-time loop, creating a fresh environment for people and policies to practice, explore, generate data, and evaluate what happens next.

Industry observers note that this is a fascinating leap for surgical robotics. Real-time generative simulation could greatly reduce risks in training and planning. The concept of distilling a large model into a causal student model is clever. If you're also exploring video generation from images, check out the Seedance 2.5 image-to-video tool for creative applications.

Assessing more than just visual quality is the immediate next step. A practical surgical simulator must enable findings that translate to the real robot, maintain instrument and scene organization during extended rollouts, and react appropriately to actions. Tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action variety, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and actual policy outcomes are some of the new closed-loop benchmarks that are motivated by this.

The progress in surgical robotics is genuinely exciting! 🏥🤖 Being able to train and test advanced vision-language-action systems in realistic simulations without risking expensive equipment or delicate procedures could make development much faster and safer. The level of detail needed for tissues, instruments, smoke, and lighting really indicates how challenging this field is. 👏.

It’s impressive to see technology moving beyond simple teleoperation and towards smarter, more capable robotic assistance. 🚀 Better simulation environments can help researchers refine these systems before they ever reach an operating room, which is a win for both surgeons and patients. 😊📱.

Sources indicate that looking forward to seeing how projects like NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams shape the future of healthcare. 🌍💙 If these simulations continue becoming more realistic, they could play a huge role in improving surgical training, reducing costs, and ultimately delivering better patient outcomes. Amazing work and an exciting glimpse into what's ahead! 🙌✨.

  • Schofield found the CFTC was unlikely to show that the Commodity Exchange Act overrides state gambling laws.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two federal judges have now declined to protect Kalshi from New York's state-court gambling enforcement. The case moves to a state judge, and Kalshi disputes how far the proposed order would reach beyond New York.

U.S. District Judge Lorna Schofield denied the CFTC’s renewed emergency request on Friday, November 20, after a telephone hearing that began at 5 p.m. ET, ruling from the bench in Manhattan.

Schofield found the CFTC was unlikely to show that the Commodity Exchange Act overrides state gambling laws. That includes licensing rules applied to prediction market operators. Her ruling came a day after Judge Vernon Broderick sent the case back to state court.

The agency’s earlier bid had gone before U.S. District Judge Jed Rakoff.

With the federal route closed for now, the case sits with Justice Melissa Crane of New York County Supreme Court.

The proposed order would bar Kalshi from running an unlicensed gambling business within or from New York, or for people in the state. It covers sports, culture, election and other event contracts. It would also block customers under 21 from trading.

Sources indicate that the reach of that language is Kalshi’s central concern. In a Thursday-night letter to Crane, Kalshi’s Milbank lawyer Sean Murphy warned that the order would close the exchange to all customers everywhere, because the company is based in Newly introduced York. The letter also pointed to the likely forced liquidation of all open positions. James’s office has said that shutting Kalshi down nationwide is not what it is after.

In a recent development, the CFTC has tried to place event contracts beyond state reach. On April 24, 2026, it sued New York in the Southern District of New York. It sought a declaration that it alone regulates event contracts. Similar suits had already targeted Arizona, Connecticut and Illinois.

On August 11, the agency issued an emergency order telling Kalshi to keep performing its functions as a designated contract market. Kalshi had warned the CFTC on August 1 that Latest York’s pending motion created a market emergency. The order was meant to reassure traders that one state cannot shut down a CFTC-registered exchange.

The financial exposure is large. Upcoming York seeks a permanent injunction and full restitution to users. It also wants a $100,000 penalty for each attempt to offer sports wagering, plus a further penalty of three times Kalshi’s gains.

The case lands on top of a 3-1 run of federal appeals court rulings against Kalshi. That record raises the chance the Supreme Court takes up whether states can regulate prediction markets. Separately, the Second Circuit denied relief on November 3 in Kalshi’s own suit against Latest York regulators.

Sources indicate that the Attorney General’s office has a track record in this area. It sued Coinbase and Gemini in April 2026. In June 2025, it shut down 26 illegal online sweepstakes casinos.

Whether Fresh York gets the restraining order it wants is now up to Crane.

#161386. GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft

📅 30 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2677 w)

GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft

📅 30 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2677 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, aviation learned this the hard way.
  • Industry observers note that the reason is structural.
  • It has been revealed that A bigger fleet still helps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, aviation learned this the hard way. For most of the industry's history, the number that best predicted whether an airline would survive was how much of the day each aircraft spent on the ground.

Industry observers note that the reason is structural. An aircraft's costs accrue by the calendar hour: financing, depreciation, hull insurance, scheduled maintenance, crew contracts. Its revenue accrues only by the flight hour. Every hour spent on the ground shrinks the output side of that equation while the cost side keeps running exactly as before. Utilization also sits downstream of almost everything else an airline does. Turnaround discipline, network design, maintenance planning, crew rostering, and spare parts availability all eventually show up in that one number, because a broken operation underneath it keeps planes on the ground no matter what else goes right.

It has been revealed that A bigger fleet still helps. More aircraft means more available capacity, plainly and simply. But two airlines flying comparable fleets on comparable routes can end up with very different economics, and most of that gap traces back to one measurement rather than fleet size.

Sources indicate that enterprise AI is running into the same structure, on a different piece of hardware. A GPU accrues cost by the calendar hour too, through financing, depreciation, power, and cooling, whether or not it's doing anything useful in a given moment. Its output only accrues by the compute hour. More GPUs helps in roughly the way a bigger fleet helps an airline: real capacity, a genuine advantage, and still no guarantee of the result that actually decides who wins. Two companies with comparable GPU budgets increasingly diverge based on how much of that hardware is doing something useful at any given moment, not on how much of it either one owns. That same number, like an airline's utilization rate, sits downstream of nearly every other infrastructure decision a company makes. Intelligence has carried the industry this far. Utilization is where the next real constraint is forming.

It has been revealed that the scarcity didn't disappear as AI scaled. It moved up the chain, landing on a different resource entirely.

According to recent reports, the first wave of enterprise AI was won on model quality. Bigger models, trained on more compute, evaluated against tougher benchmarks: parameter count and leaderboard position dominated the conversation, and the race produced models genuinely good enough to run real enterprise workloads. That capability arrives bundled with a dependency, though. Production AI runs on specialized hardware, and today that hardware is almost entirely GPUs.

According to recent reports, GPUs are expensive, supply constrained, and in demand far beyond what's available, and this holds even at the very top of the market. In 2020, Microsoft built OpenAI a dedicated supercomputer: over 10,000 GPUs and 285,000 CPU cores, reported at the time as one of the five largest systems in the world, assembled to train what became GPT-3. At the time, it looked like an almost unimaginable concentration of hardware, the kind of number that made compute look like a solved problem for whoever could get access to it. Six years later, that number reads more like a starting point than a ceiling. By 2026, even the best capitalized labs on the planet were treating compute access as a live strategic constraint rather than a settled one. Anthropic alone was running simultaneous multi-gigawatt commitments across four separate hardware platforms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and AMD, layered within months of one another, while Meta signed a comparable multi-gigawatt deal of its own. Spreading commitments across four vendors at once is what compute scarcity looks like when a buyer has effectively unlimited capital and still can't get enough from any single source.

In a recent development, six years apart, both events marked the frontier of what a lab needed just to stay competitive. What changed in between has less to do with AI getting more capable, and everything to do with capability no longer being the binding constraint.

The same pattern shows up downstream of the labs, in a different form. Enterprises consuming these models through an API run into a pricing problem more than a hardware one. Cost scales linearly with tokens used, and that single fact separates the economics of a proof of concept from the economics of production almost completely. A PoC processing a few thousand requests a month looks affordable. The same workload at production volume can turn into a cost line that never quite clears. The alternative gaining ground is straightforward enough: enterprises acquiring their own GPUs and running models locally, trading a variable, linearly scaling cost for a fixed capital one.

API cost rises with usage, while owned infrastructure stays close to fixed. Past the breakeven point, the trade reverses.

That shift turns the GPU into infrastructure rather than a line item, sized for growth, sized for demand peaks, and therefore sized above what any given week actually needs. Which means the purchase doesn't close the problem. It opens a new one. The day the cluster comes online, the question stops being can we get accelerators and becomes can we keep them busy, and only the first question had a procurement team assigned to it. Signing for the hardware is the part with a deadline and an owner. Keeping it off the ground is the part that quietly decides whether the deal was worth signing.

These deals describe capacity commitments, not efficiency. How well that capacity gets used is a separate question, owned by different people, measured far less rigorously, and considerably further from being solved.

Industry observers note that A cluster full of busy GPUs can still be wasting most of its potential, and the reason is almost always the same one. GPUs run continuously, day and night, while the demand placed on them does not. Infrastructure has to be sized for the peak, the moment training runs, batch jobs, and real time traffic all land at once, which leaves a meaningful share of capacity provisioned and unused outside that peak. Better forecasting could solve that on its own if every GPU could absorb every kind of work equally well. Few can, and that turns out to be the harder half of the problem.

The mismatch begins one layer deeper.

According to recent reports, in the first generation of enterprise AI, a GPU's job was largely singular: run inference. Today the same hardware supports training, fine-tuning, quantization, real-time inference, batch inference, embedding generation, and model evaluation, often for the same organization, sometimes for the same model, on the same cluster. Each of these workloads wants something different from the hardware, and the differences run deep. Real-time inference needs low latency above nearly everything else, because a slow response counts as a failed one. Batch work cares about throughput and tolerates delay, sometimes for hours. Training can occupy a GPU continuously for a stretch measured in hours or days. Quantization needs a large amount of capacity, but only briefly. A scheduler tuned for one of these will misallocate the other three almost by default. The failure doesn't always show up on a utilization dashboard either. A cluster can report high average occupancy while several queued jobs wait for a GPU shape that happens to be busy running something else entirely.

Recent findings suggest that the exact workload mix varies by organization. The shape of the problem does not. This is also where the aircraft analogy runs into its limit, and the limit teaches something rather than just qualifying the comparison. An idle aircraft can usually be redeployed to any route in the fleet: a 737 sitting in Chicago can fly to Denver instead of Dallas without much penalty. An idle GPU can only absorb a workload whose memory, latency, and duration profile it can actually serve. That difference makes orchestration harder than fleet scheduling, and it's why the question stops being whether GPUs are occupied and turns into which workload should run on which GPU, at what time, with what priority. Buying another rack of GPUs adds capacity and cost, not a fix for the mismatch, and that new capacity can sit in the wrong shape at the wrong moment just as easily as the capacity already installed.

It has been revealed that maximizing GPU ROI takes more than a one-time provisioning decision. It calls for continuous, active management of the infrastructure itself, running every hour rather than only at procurement time. What's emerging in response is a distinct discipline, GPU Management, an orchestration layer sitting between workloads, models, and hardware. Its job is to decide, continuously, which workload runs, when it runs, how it runs, and on which specific GPU in the cluster. None of this is exotic in concept. It's closer to what a good operations team already does by instinct, just formalized and running continuously instead of depending on someone noticing a problem.

According to recent reports, intelligence doesn't stop at the model boundary. The orchestration layer is making real-time allocation decisions the model itself has no visibility into.

Intelligence used to sit almost entirely in the model: bigger, better trained, more capable, and that was most of the game. Now it also has to sit in the infrastructure, in the layer deciding, moment to moment, which of several competing workloads gets the GPU that just freed up, and at what priority relative to everything else waiting in the queue. Keeping GPUs busy stops being the goal on its own, since busy is easy to fake by running low priority work that could have waited. Maximizing the return generated by each installed GPU becomes the actual target, and that turns out to be a far more continuous problem than the provisioning question that came before it.

Provisioning well doesn't make this go away so much as change its shape. A provisioning decision gets made once, at purchase time. An allocation decision gets made constantly: every time a job finishes, every newly introduced request that arrives, every shift in priority between a customer facing service and an internal training run. That frequency explains why the decision has moved from something a person handles case by case into something that has to run automatically. No engineer is watching a dashboard at three in the morning to decide whether a finished training run should hand its GPU to a queued batch job or hold it for an incoming burst of customer traffic. Something else has to make that call, continuously, and make it correctly often enough that nobody needs to check.

It has been revealed that the discipline is latest enough that its tooling and conventions are still forming, and no single playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. What has settled, at least, is where the constraint moved.

Specialization and orchestration solve different halves of the same problem.

Sources indicate that specialized, smaller models can perform specific tasks at a fraction of the resource cost a large generalist model would need for the same job, without giving up the quality the task requires. That has a direct effect on utilization. Workloads that once required a single, large model, occupying a large share of a cluster's capacity for the full duration of the job, can instead run on smaller, task-specific models occupying a fraction of that footprint. Capacity that used to be entirely spoken for is suddenly free.

According to recent reports, how much capacity specialization frees varies by workload and model, but the freed capacity still has to go somewhere or it just sits there. A smaller specialized model only converts into GPU ROI if something is actively deciding what happens next with the space it frees up, reallocating it to another workload, another model, another queue waiting behind it. Left unmanaged, freed capacity becomes a different flavor of idle rather than a win, invisible in a different way than an obviously unused GPU, but no more productive.

Recent findings suggest that specialization without orchestration frees capacity nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming. Neither lever does the whole job alone.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity that nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming in the first place, because the models are still large and the footprint they leave behind is small. Neither lever does the whole job alone; each one raises the ceiling on what the other lever can achieve. Neither is optional if the goal is to actually close the gap between installed capacity and useful output, rather than shifting where the waste happens to sit.

Sources indicate that this is why model architecture and GPU management are two ways to address the same problem, approached from two different directions that end up leaning on each other. One shrinks what each workload needs. The other decides, continuously, where the difference goes.

A bigger fleet has always been a real advantage, and nothing here argues otherwise. Among airlines with comparable fleets, sometimes even a smaller one facing a larger rival, the winner was usually whichever one flew what it had more completely, carrying the weight of everything the airline did well underneath it. Enterprise AI is arriving at the same discipline from a different direction. GPUs are already installed, already depreciating, already committed. Specialized models and GPU Management are parallel solutions, or bivalent strategies. Specialization shrinks what each workload needs. Management maximizes the return on infrastructure. Enterprises that master both will set the pace of AI competition for the next decade.

The next frontier is managing an entire fleet of agents and there is nothing stopping it.

Industry observers note that agreed. And the part that isn't priced in yet: a fleet of agents makes per-token cost scale linearly with the business. At some point large enterprises stop paying that curve and bring the models in-house — which doesn't remove the cost, it just trades a vendor price list for a utilization number. And agent fleets are brutal on utilization: real-time inference under latency SLAs, batch jobs, retraining, evals — all bursty, all fighting over the same finite pool. Managing the fleet is going to be, in large part, a GPU scheduling problem.

Scheduling is the core bottleneck of this problem. A CPU-like isolation mechanism, or a sandbox-based architecture on GPUs, could significantly alleviate this problem.

According to recent reports, good point, isolation is a real part of the picture. CPU-style boundaries (and the GPU sandboxing now landing, like the Kata Containers work) are what make it safe to co-locate unrelated workloads on the same card without fault or memory-contention risk, which widens the set of placements a scheduler is even allowed to make.

Taking that a step further: once co-location is safe, we have to decide which workload runs on which GPU, at what time, at what priority, given that each one wants something different from the hardware (memory footprint, latency tolerance, duration). Isolation gives you a bigger, safer decision space; something still has to pick the right point in it. And rigid partitioning can even cut utilization, since an idle slice can't lend capacity to a busy neighbor.

That's exactly the direction we're taking next: an intelligent solution for job scheduling. We've got a follow-up article on it in the works, which will be published next week. Would be curious to get your read when it's out.

It has been revealed that I expect we will see GPU rental systems become a thing. There are a lot of high-end GPUs sitting in consumer computers doing absolutely nothing for 90% of the day. Imagine if individuals could allow a training model to access their GPU remotely and in return pay them something in return. Yes, remote GPUs is not optimal, but with the consumer taking on the maintenance, power bill, and ownership of the GPU, any use the training model gets is a net positive.

We're thrilled to share that Baseten is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub!

It has been revealed that baseten joins our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub's model pages. Inference Providers are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for both JS and Python), making it super easy to use a wide variety of models with your preferred providers.

In a recent development, baseten is an AI infrastructure platform that covers serverless AI, training and more. With a catalog of many frontier models, Baseten makes it easy for developers to integrate a wide range of AI capabilities into their applications with minimal setup.

Baseten supports a broad spectrum of model types - from LLMs to text-to-speech and more. As part of this initial integration, Baseten is launching support for conversational and text-generation tasks on Hugging Face, enabling access to popular open-weight LLMs such as Kimi K3, latest DeepSeek V4 Flash, GLM-5.2, and many more. Support for additional tasks will roll out soon!

See the full list of models supported by Baseten here.

Follow Baseten on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/baseten.

Baseten is available through the Hugging Face SDKs - huggingface_hub (>= 1.26.1) for Python and @huggingface/inference for JavaScript.

For direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a baseten API key you're billed on your baseten account.

It has been revealed that for routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the Hugging Face Hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us; we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.).

Crucial Note ‼️ PRO owners get $2 worth of Inference credits every month. You can use them across providers. 🔥.
